Group 9 · Going for the Gold · Introduction to Statistics

Weather moves the field.
History helps predict the runner.

Six real-world Kaggle datasets turn a one-city analysis into a study of weather, race context, pacing, and what we can actually know before the finish.

Berlin · Chicago · Boston · U.S. fall marathons
Six datasets analyzed; a seventh training dataset audited and excluded from substantive inference.

SourcesHeatHumidity & windRace fieldsPacingPredictionHome weatherTraining logsClassmate questionsMethods

A marathon’s finishing time reflects both the person and the day. Our initial Berlin analysis found that warmer years were slower on average, but demographics and weather predicted individuals poorly. Expanding the evidence reveals why those conclusions can coexist: weather shifts a field’s average, while information about the runner’s previous performance or current pace is far more useful for predicting that runner.

5.3 min / 5°CChicago’s standardized annual mean is slower on warmer mornings.
95% CI: 1.8–8.8 minutes.
27.8 → 15.1 minPrediction MAE falls when we use the previous finish instead of demographics in matched Boston repeaters.
36.7 minutes90th–10th percentile spread between adjusted race-field means across 21 retained races.

These are observational results. The source counts overlap and must not be added into a unique-runner total. Prediction comparisons use the same test runners within each analysis, not across unrelated populations.

More data must add information, not just rows

We analyzed six Kaggle datasets and inspected several alternatives. Chicago adds a second long weather record and dew point/wind. Boston adds split times, cautious repeat-runner matches, and recent weather near runners’ homes. The fall-marathon sample adds event diversity. A large daily-log source adds actual recorded training, with a carefully qualified race-day outcome. The sources have different measurement definitions and sampling rules, so we use them for complementary analyses rather than concatenate everything.

The source audit changed the analysis in concrete ways. Berlin’s 2019 file contains only male runners, so the initial study ends in 2018. Chicago’s “Age” is an age-group upper boundary, not an exact birthday age. Chicago 2007 was stopped mid-race, so that year is excluded from the primary weather fit and restored in sensitivity analysis. For Boston 2024, padding ZIP codes to five characters increases matching records from 11,857 to 17,191; 29 remain unmatched. We then exclude all 22 rows belonging to 11 duplicated bib numbers with conflicting results, rather than guess which is correct. The weather file also includes race day itself, which we remove to preserve a genuinely pre-race window.

Chicago 2010–2019 also appears in the fall-marathon sample. It contributes to two different questions, but not two independent replications of the same weather claim. Public result records may contain repeat people; no claim here counts them as unique runners.

1. The heat signal survives a second city

The original Berlin cohort contains 629,545 finishes over 20 years. Its standardized annual mean is associated with 6.5 extra minutes per 5°C in daily average temperature (95% CI 4.2–8.7). Chicago supplies a separate event history: 852,085 eligible finishes over 26 uninterrupted race years.

For each city, we first compare annual means at a fixed age/sex composition, then adjust for a linear calendar trend. Chicago’s corresponding estimate is 5.3 minutes per 5°C (95% CI 1.8–8.8; p = 0.004). The model has 26 weather observations, not hundreds of thousands: all runners in a year share the event’s recorded weather.

Chicago’s estimate remains positive when individual years are omitted: slopes range from 4.5 to 6.3 minutes per 5°C. The notebook also reports 2007 inclusion, a quadratic trend, additional weather adjustment, exclusion of 2021, and a 9 a.m./noon temperature average. These checks assess fragility; they do not remove unmeasured changes in entrants, timing, or race organization.

The evidence is stronger than a single-city finding, but it is still an association among recorded finishers. Heat-related non-finishes are absent. In particular, the 2007 race stoppage illustrates why finishers alone cannot reveal the full consequences of extreme conditions.

2. Humidity and wind are addressable—but not precisely resolved

The Chicago weather file contains air temperature and dew point. We use the EPA-documented Magnus approximation to derive relative humidity. This extends the original proposal beyond temperature. It is an estimated humidity measure, not a humidity column directly measured in the source.

With temperature, year trend, estimated RH, and wind in the same annual model, the humidity estimate is -0.83 minutes per 10 percentage points of RH, but its 95% interval runs from -4.33 to 2.67. Wind is similarly imprecise. The data therefore do not distinguish a separate humidity or wind association with useful confidence.

Chicago comparisonEstimate and 95% CI
Chicago: temperature, minutes per 5°C5.33 (1.84 to 8.81)
Chicago: temperature adjusted for RH/wind, per 5°C5.54 (1.17 to 9.90)
Chicago: RH, minutes per 10 percentage points-0.83 (-4.33 to 2.67)
Chicago: wind, minutes per 5 source units-0.30 (-4.25 to 3.65)

The file does not label units. We interpret temperature and dew point as Fahrenheit, consistent with their values and U.S. source conventions, then convert to Celsius; this remains a documented source assumption. Wind stays in its recorded units instead of asserting a per-mph interpretation. Temperature and atmospheric moisture covary, and 26 race days give limited room to separate them. A wide interval is not evidence that humidity or wind do not matter.

3. Demographics explain only part of the difference between races

The broad fall dataset contains 2,053,366 recorded results from 96 named races. For stable comparisons, we retain race-years with at least ten finishes in every age-decade/sex group from ages 20–69 and races with at least eight such years. That leaves 1,624,823 results across 199 events and 21 races.

We standardize race-year means to a common demographic mix and adjust for year indicators. The 90th–10th percentile spread between race means is 38.2 minutes before adjustment and 36.7 after adjustment. Large differences remain.

That remaining spread is statistically interesting precisely because age and sex cannot explain it away. It may reflect elevation, weather, time limits, charity participation, runner preparation, or who chooses each event. We cannot assign it to terrain without course and selection data. The analysis answers “do the fields still differ?” rather than “how many minutes does this course cause?”

The original demographic findings remain useful context: in Berlin, the age-standardized female-minus-male mean difference is 27.1 minutes, and the sex-standardized 60–64-minus-30–34 contrast is 30.1 minutes. Those are group differences, not deterministic rules about individuals.

4. Boston shows how finishing time is accumulated

The three Boston files contain 79,638 results, of which 79,576 meet the halfway-comparison rules. We calculate the percentage increase in time from the first half to the second. A value of 10 means the second half took 10% longer. It does not establish that a runner physiologically “hit the wall.”

The adjusted male-minus-female slowdown contrasts range from 2.2 to 6.4 percentage points across the three editions. Comparing equal halfway times does not isolate physiology: it conditions on a variable already shaped by ability, pacing, terrain, and conditions.

These profiles move the analysis beyond a single finish-time column. They show when the field slows, and how the pattern varies between editions. They do not by themselves tell runners what pacing strategy would cause a faster finish.

5. Better information helps more than a more elaborate demographic model

The original Berlin prediction model had about 35 minutes of mean absolute error on future race years. The expanded data let us ask a more practical question: what information was missing?

Before the race: use a previous performance

We conservatively match Boston runners using normalized name, recorded sex, country, and a birth-year proxy; ambiguous keys are excluded. We train on 5,516 matched 2015→2016 transitions and evaluate on 4,922 matched 2016→2017 transitions. These are probable links, not verified identities. The population is repeat finishers, not all entrants.

In the held-out transition, demographics alone have an MAE of 27.8 minutes. Simply predicting the previous finish gives 15.1 minutes. That is a 12.7-minute reduction; a paired bootstrap over the held-out matches gives a 95% interval of 12.0–13.4 minutes. That interval is conditional on this event and these matches, not uncertainty over every possible future marathon.

Before-race model2017 MAE (min)2017 R²
Repeat previous finish15.140.709
Demographics27.840.195
Demographics + previous finish15.760.734

A location-agreement sensitivity check additionally requires the same city and state. Previous race time is a useful proxy for demonstrated performance, but it is not a measurement of training mileage or years of experience. We retain the simple previous-time baseline even when it beats calibration.

After 10 km: current pace changes the prediction problem

We separately train on 2015–2016 and test on 2017, predicting time remaining after 10 km. Predicting the remaining time avoids giving the model a mechanical advantage from an outcome that contains the observed checkpoint. A learned model with demographics and the first 10 km has an MAE of 13.0 minutes, versus 24.3 for demographics alone.

After-10-km modelRemaining-time MAE (min)R²
Training remaining-time mean27.13-0.038
Constant 10-km pace22.270.331
Demographics24.310.109
Demographics + first 10 km13.000.718

The notebook also evaluates the checkpoint models on 2017 records with no identity-proxy match in training. No final rank, projected finish derived from later data, or later split is used. The gain comes from relevant available information, not from pretending that a halfway or finishing-time feature was known before the race.

6. Home weather does not give a clear acclimatization answer

For Boston 2024, we link 17,169 U.S. runners to 14 days of weather at 5,878 home ZIP codes. We exclude race day, preserve leading zeros, report 29 unmatched runners, exclude 22 conflicting-bib rows, and cluster uncertainty by 751 ZIP prefixes.

The primary adjusted estimate is 0.16 slowdown percentage points per 5°C warmer home weather (95% CI -0.14 to 0.47; p = 0.298). The interval includes zero, and the estimated direction changes with adjustment. This proxy does not show a clear protective association.

Home-weather specificationSlowdown points per 5°C (95% CI)
Unadjusted-0.18 (-0.54 to 0.18)
Age and sex only-0.26 (-0.64 to 0.11)
Age, sex, first-half time0.16 (-0.14 to 0.47)
Cluster by individual ZIP0.16 (-0.09 to 0.41)
Mean daily minimum temperature0.18 (-0.14 to 0.49)
Include conflicting bib records0.16 (-0.14 to 0.47)

We cannot infer that acclimatization is ineffective. Home temperature does not tell us where someone trained, whether they used a treadmill, when they traveled, or how much heat exposure they had. First-half-time adjustment also changes the estimand. This is an informative limit of an available proxy, not an excuse to force a positive finding.

7. Actual training logs change what we can study

Continuing beyond the flawed 87-row pilot led to a more substantive source: a Kaggle mirror of published running-log research data. Its 2019 daily file contains 13,290,380 athlete-day rows for 36,412 anonymous athletes, including zero-activity days. These are daily records, not that many runs or independent runners.

We extract 56 strictly pre-race days for athletes labeled as Boston 2019 or Chicago 2019 participants. Recorded weekly distance, running days per week, and average training pace are now available. We exclude inconsistent training windows and require a marathon-like distance on the labeled event day. The retained analysis has 5,247 athlete-event records.

The outcome is different: this source has daily logged duration, not a certified finish time. We restrict the race-day total to 40–46 km and 120–480 minutes, but warm-up, cool-down, recording differences, and missing uploads remain possible. This analysis is supplementary and must not be presented as an official marathon-finish prediction.

In the age/sex/event-adjusted comparison, 10 additional logged km/week are associated with -8.3 minutes in the race-day duration proxy (95% CI -8.7 to -7.9). With average training pace also included, the estimate is -4.8 minutes (95% CI -5.1 to -4.5). This does not show that prescribing extra mileage causes that improvement: ability, health, and logging behavior may affect both.

For a prediction check, we fit on Boston 2019 and evaluate on Chicago 2019, removing 55 overlapping athlete IDs from the test set. Demographics alone give an MAE of 56.8 minutes; adding recorded volume, frequency, and training pace gives 21.8 minutes on the same 1022 new-athlete test records. These are errors for the logged-duration proxy, not errors comparable with the official-result models above.

Mileage and running-day frequency correlate at 0.91, so we do not claim their separate causal importance. Sensitivity checks require at least six active weeks or narrow the race-day distance gate to 40–44 km. The public source uses coarse, estimated ages and social-network users with major-marathon history; it is not representative of every runner. Matching these logs to official finishes would be the next substantive improvement.

Where the classmates’ questions now stand

Classmate questionEvidence now availableWhat remains unknown
Different races or years?Berlin + Chicago weather analyses; 21 comparable fall-race fieldsNot a random sample of all marathons
Humidity and wind?Chicago dew point permits estimated RH; wind is in the sourceSeparate effects remain imprecise; wind units undocumented
Course difficulty or terrain?Age/sex/year-adjusted differences between race fieldsElevation/course effects cannot be isolated from selection and weather
Training frequency and experience?Actual 8-week running logs plus previous Boston performanceLogging incompleteness, coarse ages, proxy outcome; years of experience unmeasured
Climate acclimatization?Boston 2024 home-weather proxy with 14 strictly pre-race daysActual outdoor training, travel, and acclimatization are unmeasured
Age–weather interaction?Berlin interaction tested; interval includes no differenceAge-specific heat tolerance is not established
Outliers?Valid extremes retained; trimming sensitivity; split arithmetic auditedExtreme values cannot all be individually verified
Prediction on unseen years?Berlin 2014–2018, Boston 2017 held outSome runners recur; identity linkage is imperfect
Other weather, including rain?Berlin precipitation sensitivity; Chicago wind/humidityHarmonized hourly route-level exposures still absent

A small training dataset looked promising but did not survive the audit: 87 records, 74 missing cross-training entries, an implausibly large speed value, and documentation stating that mileage includes the marathon itself. We did not train a supposedly pre-race model on that contaminated feature or on finish-derived outcome categories. A separate Run Club dataset explicitly describes synthetic generation, so it was excluded from real-world conclusions.

What makes these results reviewable

The executed marathon_analysis.ipynb contains the full analysis in separated explanation/code cells. The original Berlin study remains in Chapters 1–8; the expansion is in Chapters 9–15. Raw files are unchanged, versions and hashes are recorded, and every figure and summary table is exported. No individual names or ZIP codes appear in exported analytical tables or this report.

  • Weather inference: race-year observations, direct demographic standardization, calendar-trend adjustment, HC3 uncertainty, and specified sensitivity checks.
  • Cross-race comparison: minimum cell support, a common demographic distribution, and equal-year adjustment; descriptive field comparisons only.
  • Pacing: missing and non-increasing checkpoints handled by analysis-specific rules; within-year adjusted comparisons, without pretending three years identify a weather effect.
  • Prediction: later race years held out; all preprocessing fitted on training data; explicit distinction between before-race, historical, and checkpoint information.
  • Home weather: audited ZIP join, strict pre-race dates, complete exposure windows, geographic clustering, and multiple specifications.
  • Multiplicity: the original three Berlin tests retain Holm correction. The extension is exploratory; four focal weather/home-weather tests receive BH false-discovery-rate adjustment. Sensitivity checks and descriptive model comparisons are not treated as independent confirmations.

Chicago: RH, minutes per 10 percentage points-0.83 (-4.33 to 2.67)0.62810.8374

Home temperature: slowdown points per 5°C0.16 (-0.14 to 0.47)0.29820.5964

Limitations remain consequential: finishers are selected survivors of each event; names are imperfect linkage keys; weather is a coarse exposure; age classifications differ by source; recurring runners and spatial dependence may remain; and the training-log source measures recorded activity rather than verified exposure or certified race outcomes. More observations reduce some uncertainty, but cannot repair an unmeasured variable or an inappropriate comparison.
